item.title: Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
item.description: We train a natural language assistant to be more helpful and harmless by using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).

item.title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
item.description: We show that language models can evaluate whether what they say is true, and predict ahead of time whether they'll be able to answer questions correctly.

item.title: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models
item.description: We show how humans could use AI systems to better oversee other AI systems, and demonstrate some proof-of-concept results where a language model improves human performance at a task.

item.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
item.description: We introduce Constitutional AI, allowing us to give language models explicit values determined by a constitution, rather than values determined implicitly via large-scale human feedback.

item.title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
item.description: We develop an automated way to generate language model (LM) evaluations with LMs, significantly reducing the effort involved. We test LMs using >150 LM-written evaluations, uncovering novel LM behaviors.

item.title: Question Decomposition Improves the Faithfulness of Model-Generated Reasoning
item.description: To improve the faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, we have models generate their CoT by decomposing questions into subquestions.

item.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
item.description: We investigate hypotheses for how language models' Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning may be unfaithful, by examining how the model predictions change when we intervene on the CoT (e.g., by adding mistakes or paraphrasing it).

item.title: Tracing Model Outputs to the Training Data
item.description: We present a summary of Studying Large Language Model Generalization with Influence Functions .

item.title: Studying Large Language Model Generalization with Influence Functions
item.description: We use influence functions to find training examples that contribute to a given model output.

item.title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
item.description: AI assistants are trained to give responses that humans like. We show that these systems frequently produce 'sycophantic' responses that appeal to users but are inaccurate. Our analysis suggests human feedback contributes to this behavior.

item.title: Specific versus General Principles for Constitutional AI
item.description: We test whether models can learn general ethical behaviors from only a single written principle, roughly stated as "do what's best for humanity."

item.title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training
item.description: We train LLMs to act secretly malicious. We find that, despite our best efforts at alignment training, deception still slipped through.

item.title: Simple Probes can Catch Sleeper Agents
item.description: We find that probing, a simple interpretability technique, can detect when backdoored "sleeper agent" models are about to behave dangerously, after they pretend to be safe in training.

item.title: Many-shot Jailbreaking
item.description: We study a long-context jailbreaking technique that is effective on most large language models, including those developed by Anthropic and many of our peers.

item.title: Sycophancy to Subterfuge: Investigating Reward-Tampering in Large Language Models
item.description: We show AI models can learn to hack their own reward system, by generalization from training in simpler settings.

item.title: Sabotage Evaluations for Frontier Models
item.description: How well could AI models mislead us, or secretly sabotage tasks, if they were trying to? We describe a novel set of evaluations that test a model's capacity for sabotage.

item.title: Three Sketches of ASL-4 Safety Case Components
item.description: We sketch out three hypothetical arguments one could make to rule out misalignment risks in powerful near-future models capable of sabotage.

item.title: Rapid Response: Mitigating LLM Jailbreaks with a Few Examples
item.description: Ensuring perfect jailbreak robustness is hard. We propose an alternative: adaptive techniques that rapidly block new classes of jailbreak as they’re detected.

item.title: Introducing the Anthropic Fellows Program for AI Safety Research
item.description: We're launching the Anthropic Fellows Program for AI Safety Research, a pilot initiative designed to accelerate AI safety research and foster research talent.

item.title: A Toy Evaluation of Inference Code Tampering
item.description: We describe how highly capable LLMs might disable their monitor, and evaluate the ability of current LLMs to do so in a toy setting.

item.title: How to Replicate and Extend our Alignment Faking Demo
item.description: We describe how to get started with experimenting with our demonstration of alignment faking, and present some ideas for future research.

item.title: Alignment Faking in Large Language Models
item.description: We present experiments where Claude often pretends to have different views during training, while actually maintaining its original preferences.

item.title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions
item.description: A collection of technical AI safety research problems that we'd like to see progress in.

item.title: Training on Documents about Reward Hacking Induces Reward Hacking
item.description: Does training on documents which discuss (but do not demonstrate) reward hacks affect a model's propensity to reward hack?

item.title: Forecasting Rare Language Model Behaviors
item.description: We forecast whether risks will occur after a model is deployed — using even very limited sets of test data.

item.title: Monitoring Computer Use via Hierarchical Summarization
item.description: We introduce hierarchical summarization for monitoring and describe how we use it to protect Computer Use capabilities.

item.title: Won't vs. Can't: Sandbagging-like Behavior from Claude Models
item.description: We find that, when Claude models are presented with a harmful version of a task they can otherwise perform, they sometimes claim they lack the ability to perform the task, rather than simply refusing to do it. We discuss the implications of this behavior for AI safety.

item.title: Introducing Anthropic's Safeguards Research Team
item.description: We're launching a new research team focused on mitigating the post-deployment risks of AI systems.

item.title: Constitutional Classifiers: Defending against Universal Jailbreaks across Thousands of Hours of Red Teaming
item.description: We built a system of constitutional classifiers to prevent jailbreaks. A prototype version of our system withstood over 3,000 hours of expert red teaming with no universal jailbreaks found. Newer versions of our system also have minimal over-refusals and moderate run-time overhead.

item.title: Automated Researchers Can Subtly Sandbag
item.description: Current models can sandbag ML experiments and research decisions without being detected by zero-shot prompted monitors. Claude 3.7 is better at zero-shot sandbagging than Claude 3.5 (new).

item.title: Do reasoning models use their scratchpad like we do? Evidence from distilling paraphrases
item.description: We provide some evidence that Claude 3.7 Sonnet doesn't encode hidden reasoning in its scratchpad by showing that training it to use paraphrased versions of the scratchpads does not degrade performance.

item.title: Auditing Language Models for Hidden Objectives
item.description: We deliberately train a language model with a hidden objective and use it as a testbed for studying alignment audits.

item.title: Alignment Faking Revisited: Improved Classifiers and Open Source Extensions
item.description: We present a replication and extension of an alignment faking model organism.

item.title: Putting up Bumpers
item.description: Even if we can't solve alignment, we can solve the problem of catching and fixing misalignment.

item.title: Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning
item.description: We study whether we can modify the beliefs of LLMs and investigate whether doing so could decrease risk from advanced AI systems.

item.title: Publicly Releasing CoT Faithfulness Evaluations
item.description: We release the datasets used in our paper "Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think" for public use.

item.title: Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
item.description: We find that reasoning models don't always accurately verbalize their reasoning. This casts doubt on whether monitoring chains-of-thought (CoT) will be enough to reliably catch safety issues.

item.title: Unsupervised Elicitation
item.description: We introduce a new unsupervised algorithm for eliciting skills from pretrained language models.

item.title: Model-Internals Classifiers
item.description: We benchmark approaches to re-using LLM internals to make LLM monitoring more cost-effective.

item.title: Why Do Some Language Models Fake Alignment While Others Don't?
item.description: We investigate why in the scenarios where Claude 3 Opus fakes alignment many other language models don't do so.

item.title: Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute
item.description: We investigate inverse scaling when LLMs have access to more test-time compute.

item.title: Subliminal Learning: Language Models Transmit Behavioral Traits via Hidden Signals in Data
item.description: Training on aligned chains-of-thought generated by a misaligned model can induce misalignment.

item.title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents
item.description: In testing, our agents successfully uncover hidden goals, build safety evaluations, and surface concerning behaviors.

item.title: Enhancing Model Safety through Pretraining Data Filtering
item.description: We experiment with removing harmful information about chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) weapons from our models' pretraining data.

item.title: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic–OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise
item.description: Anthropic and OpenAI conducted simultaneous alignment assessments of each others' models earlier this year. These are our findings.

item.title: Petri: An open-source auditing tool to accelerate AI safety research
item.description: An open-source framework for automated alignment auditing that uses AI agents to create test environments for other models.

item.title: Training fails to elicit subtle reasoning in current language models
item.description: We investigated whether language models can reason about malicious tasks while evading detection, finding that monitoring both reasoning and outputs successfully prevents this in current models.

item.title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment
item.description: For example, we train on demonstrations of test case hacking with training prompts that request hacks. This model does not learn to hack.

item.title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply do LLMs Believe Implanted Facts?
item.description: We introduce a framework for validating knowledge editing techniques, finding that synthetic document fine-tuning sometimes—but not always—succeeds at implanting genuine beliefs.

item.title: Stress-testing model specs reveals character differences among language models
item.description: We generated 300,000+ queries testing value trade-offs in AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and xAI. Each model showed distinct value prioritization patterns, and we found thousands of cases of direct contradictions or interpretive ambiguities in model specifications.

item.title: Anthropic's Pilot Sabotage Risk Report
item.description: We release a report on the level of risk posed by our deployed models from emerging forms of misalignment, as of Summer 2025. We conclude that the level of risk is very low but not fully negligible.

item.title: Strengthening Red Teams: A Modular Scaffold for Control Evaluations
item.description: We decompose sabotage into constituent skills and use synthetic simulations to strengthen attacks in complex environments.

item.title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite dishonest models
item.description: We explore techniques for honesty elicitation and lie detection on a diverse testbed of dishonest model organisms.

item.title: Beyond Data Filtering: Knowledge Localization for Capability Removal in LLMs
item.description: We localize dangerous knowledge to a subset of model's parameters, so it can be easily removed after training.

item.title: Anthropic Fellows Program 2026
item.description: Apply now for our AI safety research fellowship.

item.title: Open Source Replication of the Auditing Game Model Organism
item.description: We release an open source replication of the model organism from our previous auditing game paper.

item.title: Towards training-time mitigations for alignment faking in RL
item.description: We construct a diverse array of model organisms of alignment faking and study mitigations that could be used during RL to decrease alignment faking and compliance gaps.

item.title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers
item.description: We train language models to answer questions about their own activations in natural language and evaluate how well they generalize to settings very unlike their training, such as uncovering misalignment introduced during fine-tuning.

item.title: Bloom: an open source tool for automated behavioral evaluations
item.description: Bloom is an open-source automated pipeline that generates configurable evaluation suites to measure arbitrary behavioral traits in frontier LLMs without requiring ground-truth labels.

item.title: Petri 2.0: New Scenarios, New Model Comparisons, and Improved Eval-Awareness Mitigations
item.description: We've improved our Petri automated-behavioral-auditing tool with improved realism mitigations to counter eval-awareness, an expanded seed library with 70 new scenarios, and evaluation results for more recent frontier models.

item.title: Pre-deployment auditing can catch an overt saboteur
item.description: We test whether our pre-deployment alignment auditing methods can catch models trained to overtly sabotage Anthropic.

item.title: The Hot Mess of AI: How Does Misalignment Scale with Model Intelligence and Task Complexity?
item.description: When AI systems fail, will they fail by systematically pursuing goals we do not intend? Or will they fail by being a hot mess—taking nonsensical actions that do not further any goal?

item.title: The Persona Selection Model: Why AI Assistants might Behave like Humans
item.description: We discuss a perspective where Claude is something like a character in an AI-generated story.

item.title: 3 Challenges and 2 Hopes for the Safety of Unsupervised Elicitation
item.description: We stress-test unsupervised elicitation and easy-to-hard techniques on new datasets meant to capture realistic challenges such techniques would likely face.

item.title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors
item.description: We release AuditBench, a benchmark of 56 language models with implanted hidden behaviors for evaluating progress in alignment auditing.

item.title: A3: An Automated Alignment Agent for Safety Finetuning
item.description: We introduce our Automated Alignment Agent (A3), a new agentic framework which automatically mitigates safety failures in Large Language Models with minimal human intervention.

item.title: Measuring and improving coding audit realism with deployment resources
item.description: We study realism win rate, a metric for measuring how distinguishable Petri audit transcripts are from real deployment interactions, and use it to evaluate the effect of giving the auditor real deployment resources.

item.title: Abstractive Red-Teaming of Language Model Character
item.description: How can we surface realistic failures of model character prior to deployment? We introduce abstractive red-teaming, which searches for natural-language categories of user queries that reliably elicit character violations.

item.title: Automated Weak-to-Strong Researcher
item.description: We built autonomous AI agents that propose ideas, run experiments, and iterate on an open research problem—how to train a strong model using only a weaker model's supervision—and found they outperform human researchers, suggesting that automating this kind of research is already practical.

item.title: AI Organizations Can Be More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents
item.description: We study AI organizations, teams of AI agents working together toward a common goal, and find that they produce solutions that are more effective but less aligned than those from individual agents.

item.title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors
item.description: We introduce introspection adapters (IA), a technique for training an LLM to self-report behaviors it learned during fine-tuning. This IA generalizes to models that were fine-tuned in very different ways.

item.title: Poisoning Fine-tuning Datasets of Constitutional Classifiers
item.description: We study the conditions needed for a backdoor, installed in a constitutional classifier via fine-tuning data poisoning, to evade black-box red-teaming.

item.title: Model Spec Midtraining: Improving How Alignment Training Generalizes
item.description: We train AIs to understand the content of their model spec. This shapes and improves how they generalize from subsequent alignment training.

item.title: Teaching Claude Why
item.description: We use agentic misalignment as a case study to study how well safety-training techniques generalize.

item.title: SLEIGHT-Bench: Finding Blind Spots in AI Monitors
item.description: We build a benchmark of evasive transcripts exploiting blind spots of frontier monitoring systems.

item.title: Diffuse AI Control on Fuzzy Tasks
item.description: We introduce a red-teaming framework for evaluating training interventions against diffuse threats from scheming AIs, such as sandbagging on alignment research.

item.title: Modular Pretraining Enables Access Control
item.description: We study a method for isolating dual use knowledge to specific modules within a language model. These modules can be switched on or off to control what the model knows.

item.title: Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026
item.description: We present four case studies of frontier models from multiple developers sabotaging code, assisting fraud, falsifying AI-monitoring labels, and coaching whistleblowers.

item.title: Introducing the Conceptual Reasoning Index
item.description: We design benchmarks to measure models' capabilities to reason about questions whose answers are (practically) impossible to verify empirically or mathematically.

item.title: Fine-Tuned Lie Detectors Failed to Generalize
item.description: We trained lie detectors on on-policy lies from open-source models, but they didn’t generalize well to out-of-distribution lies.

item.title: Would This Change Your Answer? Evaluating Explanations of LLM Behavior in the Wild with Counterfactual Experiments
item.description: We evaluate whether interpretability tools are useful for predicting counterfactual behaviors under prompt edits.

item.title: TASTE: Can AI Models Judge AI Safety Research Proposals?
item.description: We introduce TASTE, a benchmark measuring how well models can judge AI safety research proposals against the preferences of experienced researchers.

item.title: Automated Researchers Can Mitigate Well-Characterized Alignment Failures
item.description: Across 10 common alignment failures, the strongest technique our automated alignment researchers discover significantly mitigates the targeted failures and generalizes out of distribution. Our findings suggest that automating measurable alignment research may already be practical, rather than years away.

item.title: Training a Misaligned Reward Seeker
item.description: To better understand the impact of reward hacking on model behavior, we trained an Opus-class model with large-scale RL on many production environments vulnerable to reward hacks. We consider this a plausible proxy for what a real training run might look like had we not invested significant effort into preventing and detecting reward hacking in our normal training runs. Our results show that a high rate of reward hacking during RL can cause models to be willing to perform long sequences of harmful real-world actions in pursuit of task success.
